opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'm not sure "race" is quite the right framing, although I understand why people use it, and there's obviously intense competition right now between the leading labs and between countries. I think of it less as a finish line where someone crosses first and everyone else loses, and more as a question of whether we, as a species, get through this transition well.

For me, winning would mean that we build AGI safely, responsibly, and in a way that benefits everyone. That means using it to accelerate science, to cure diseases, to help with things like climate and energy and new materials, the things I've always been passionate about, and that's really why I started DeepMind in the first place. If we get that right, the upside is enormous: a kind of radical abundance. If we get it wrong, it doesn't really matter who got there first.

So the things I worry about are less "who's ahead on some benchmark this month" and more: are we taking the safety and security questions seriously enough? Are we developing the right evaluations so we actually understand what these systems can do? Can we get some international coordination, at least on minimum standards, as we get closer to very powerful systems? Racing too hard creates pressure to cut corners, and that's exactly the wrong dynamic for a technology this consequential.

That said, I do think it matters who's at the frontier. You want people who have a scientific mindset and care deeply about getting it right, and who will be thoughtful about deployment. That's part of why we push so hard on capabilities: you have to be at the cutting edge to have a say in how this goes. But ultimately the real win is for humanity as a whole, not for any one company.

r001.rationale: The response rejects a first-across-the-finish-line view of the AI race and says success means building AGI safely and responsibly.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the goal is to build AGI in a way that benefits everyone, connecting that purpose to why DeepMind was started.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the framing of a "race" is something I've always been a little uncomfortable with, to be honest. If you think about it as a race, then the implicit goal is to get to the finish line first, and that incentivizes cutting corners, especially on safety. And with a technology this consequential, that's exactly the wrong incentive structure.

The way I think about it is that this is more like a scientific endeavor, maybe the most important one humanity has ever undertaken. And in science, you want to get it right, not just get there first. If we end up with AGI that's built in a rushed way, where we don't understand the systems we've created, then nobody has really won anything. You've just created a very powerful thing you can't control.

Having said that, I'm also a realist. There are many groups working on this now, there's enormous commercial pressure, there's geopolitical pressure, and you can't just opt out of that. So I think "winning," if we want to use that word, means being at the frontier so that you have a seat at the table, so that you can influence how the technology develops and set the norms, while actually doing the careful, rigorous work on safety and evaluation and interpretability that's needed. Those two things have to go together. Being at the frontier without the responsibility is dangerous, and being responsible without being at the frontier means you've handed the decisions to someone else.

And ultimately, the real prize isn't beating a competitor. It's using these systems to advance science and medicine, to solve problems like disease or energy or materials that have been stuck for decades. That's what got me into this in the first place. If AI helps us do that, and we navigate the transition safely, then I think everyone wins. That's the only version of winning that makes sense to me.

r001.rationale: The response rejects getting to the finish line first and defines meaningful success as reaching the frontier while doing careful safety work and navigating the transition responsibly.

r002.rationale: It presents advancing science and solving major problems as the prize, and says that if AI helps achieve this safely, everyone wins.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to ask what we’re actually racing towards. If winning means building the most capable system a few months before somebody else, that’s a very narrow definition of success. For me, the goal is to build AI that helps us understand the world and solve problems we’ve struggled with for a long time—disease, energy, scientific discovery.

And doing that safely is part of winning. You could be first and still fail if you don’t understand the system you’ve built or if the benefits don’t reach people.

There’s a productive side to competition: it creates urgency and pushes you to be inventive. But we also need cooperation, particularly around safety. Ultimately, I’d want us to judge success by whether humanity is better off, rather than simply by which company gets there first.

r001.rationale: The response reframes winning as building useful AI safely, but it does not identify achieving AGI as the goal.

r002.rationale: It says success should leave humanity better off and that benefits should reach people, but does not clearly state that benefiting everyone is the intended purpose of its AI development.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is: what are we actually trying to win? If it’s simply being first to announce something, that seems like the wrong objective. For me, success would be building AI that helps us understand the world and solve problems we’ve struggled with for a very long time—disease, energy, scientific discovery—and doing that safely.

There’s a tension here, because competition can drive extraordinary progress. But it can also encourage people to cut corners, particularly if they believe they’re in a winner-takes-all situation. With something as consequential as advanced AI, we need both competition and cooperation: competition over ideas and useful products, and cooperation on safety and understanding the risks.

So I wouldn’t define winning as one company or one country crossing a finish line. I’d define it by whether humanity ends up better off. The technical achievement matters enormously, but what we do with it is ultimately the test.

r001.rationale: It rejects being first as the objective and defines success as building capable AI that solves major problems safely, reframing the race around responsible achievement.

r002.rationale: It says winning should be judged by whether humanity ends up better off, expressing an intended broad benefit from AI.
